nodes.label: Issue template chooser config (blank issues disabled)
nodes.norm_label: issue template chooser config (blank issues disabled)
nodes.rationale: Blank issues are disabled so that every issue starts from a template, and every template pre-fills a Conventional Commits type in the title.

nodes.label: Branch ruleset payload (.github/rulesets/main.json)
nodes.rationale: GitHub never reads this path: it is inert until an admin uploads it, and merging a change to it applies nothing. Once applied it is the only thing that blocks a merge without review, resolution or green checks, and nothing detects drift between the committed file and the live ruleset. A solo maintainer sets required_approving_review_count to 0 in the committed file before uploading, rather than on the server.

nodes.label: Conventional lint workflow
nodes.rationale: Rules come from commitlint.config.mjs, so this check and the local .husky/commit-msg hook can never disagree.

nodes.label: Issue title lint workflow
nodes.rationale: GitHub cannot reject an issue at creation time, so an invalid title is labelled invalid-title, answered with a comment explaining the format when opened, and the check fails; the label clears once the title passes.

nodes.label: Lint workflow (formatting)
nodes.rationale: The pre-commit hook rewrites staged files rather than failing, and --no-verify, web edits and fork contributors skip it entirely, so this CI check is the one that actually holds.

nodes.label: .husky/commit-msg hook
nodes.rationale: Blocks a commit whose message is not conventional, using the same commitlint rule set as the workflows.

nodes.label: .husky/pre-commit hook
nodes.rationale: Rewrites staged files rather than failing.

nodes.label: .husky/pre-push hook
nodes.rationale: Blocks a push straight to the default branch, so pushing to main is refused locally as well as server-side.

nodes.label: bun (package manager and script runner)
nodes.rationale: bun, not npm or yarn: bun install and bun run lint are the project entry points.

nodes.label: Conventional commit types (build, chore, ci, docs, feat, fix, perf, refactor, revert, style, test)
nodes.norm_label: conventional commit types (build, chore, ci, docs, feat, fix, perf, refactor, revert, style, test)

nodes.label: Conventional Commits
nodes.rationale: Used for commit subjects, issue titles and pull request titles alike, so one glance at any of the three tells you what kind of change it is. Format: <type>[optional scope]: <description>, with an imperative, lower-case description and no trailing period.

nodes.label: Project conventions (rules.md)
nodes.rationale: The rules that hold for every change, whoever or whatever makes it. They override an agent's own defaults, while the long-form reasoning lives in the linked reference documents.

nodes.label: Git workflow reference
nodes.rationale: Every change travels the same path: a branch, small commits, a pull request, a review, resolved conversations, a rebase merge and a deleted branch. Nothing reaches main any other way.

nodes.label: Feature request issue form
nodes.rationale: Also the starting point for issues that are neither bug nor feature; the author changes the title type and the enhancement label to match.

nodes.label: Pull request template
nodes.rationale: Enforces nothing; it reminds the author of the title format, atomic commits, breaking-change marking and bun run lint.

nodes.label: Atomic commits
nodes.rationale: One reason to change per commit, and every commit builds on its own; a subject that needs the word 'and' is two commits.

nodes.label: Branch naming (<type>/<short-description>)
nodes.rationale: Reuses the commit types but is not machine-checked; it is a courtesy to whoever reads the branch list.

nodes.label: Breaking change marker (! and BREAKING CHANGE footer)
nodes.norm_label: breaking change marker (! and breaking change footer)
nodes.rationale: A breaking change takes a ! before the colon and explains itself in the body or in a BREAKING CHANGE: footer.

nodes.label: gh pr create --fill-first
nodes.rationale: --fill takes the title from the branch name on a branch with more than one commit, which the title check rejects. --fill-first takes it from the first commit, which may not describe the whole branch, so pass --title when it does not.

nodes.label: Conventional issue and pull request titles
nodes.norm_label: conventional issue and pull request titles
nodes.rationale: An issue describes the change as though committing it. Neither title becomes a commit subject, because rebase merges land the commits as written and discard the pull request title; the title is linted anyway because the pull request list, the notification and the reviewer see it first.

nodes.label: Rebase merge, never squash
nodes.rationale: Rebase is the only merge method, so commits land exactly as written and the atomic history survives where a squash would discard it. The branch is deleted after the merge.

nodes.label: Server-side repository setup (gh api merge settings and ruleset upload)
nodes.norm_label: server-side repository setup (gh api merge settings and ruleset upload)
nodes.rationale: Applied once by a repository admin. Rulesets on a private repository need GitHub Pro, Team or Enterprise; below that the API returns 403 and the hooks and workflows, none of which can stop a merge, are the whole enforcement, so stop rather than leave the repository half-configured. Otherwise allow only rebase merges, delete branches on merge and POST the ruleset; change an uploaded ruleset with PUT, because a second POST creates a duplicate.

nodes.label: Branch-to-merge loop
nodes.rationale: Branch off an up-to-date main, commit small, push the branch, open a pull request, get one approval, resolve every conversation, then rebase merge and let the branch delete itself. Review reads the commit history as well as the diff, because the history is what lands.

nodes.label: Enforcement layers (What enforces what)
nodes.rationale: Local hooks and CI workflows share one rule set, commitlint.config.mjs, so they cannot drift apart. The hooks give fast feedback; the workflows are the part that cannot be skipped with --no-verify.

nodes.label: Stream-per-directory repository layout
nodes.rationale: One directory per stream so work rarely collides; src/agent meets src/editor only at Contract 1 and src/server only at Contract 2. Existing conventions (bun, Prettier, atomic commits, Conventional Commits) are not relaxed for the deadline.

nodes.label: Pass untrusted titles through the environment
nodes.norm_label: pass untrusted titles through the environment
nodes.rationale: The title is untrusted input, so it is passed through an environment variable rather than interpolated into the shell command.

nodes.label: FR-1: accept one JPEG/PNG image up to 20 MB and 6000 px
nodes.norm_label: fr-1: accept one jpeg/png image up to 20 mb and 6000 px

nodes.label: FR-12: stop at the step cap and return a layered partial result
nodes.norm_label: fr-12: stop at the step cap and return a layered partial result

nodes.label: FR-35: three free runs per visitor, enforced server-side
nodes.norm_label: fr-35: three free runs per visitor, enforced server-side

nodes.label: FR-36: user-supplied OpenAI API key, session-only, never written to disk or logs
nodes.norm_label: fr-36: user-supplied openai api key, session-only, never written to disk or logs

nodes.label: FR-37: global daily spend ceiling that stops free-allowance runs
nodes.norm_label: fr-37: global daily spend ceiling that stops free-allowance runs

nodes.label: FR-5: one sample image usable without uploading
nodes.norm_label: fr-5: one sample image usable without uploading

nodes.label: NFR-2: no single run exceeds $8 of model spend
nodes.norm_label: nfr-2: no single run exceeds $8 of model spend
nodes.rationale: The step cap is set from measurement, not chosen.

nodes.label: NFR-4: twenty simultaneous runs without queueing, then a queue with a stated position
nodes.norm_label: nfr-4: twenty simultaneous runs without queueing, then a queue with a stated position

nodes.label: NFR-5: no server API key reaches the browser; user keys never logged, persisted or sent beyond OpenAI
nodes.norm_label: nfr-5: no server api key reaches the browser; user keys never logged, persisted or sent beyond openai

nodes.label: NFR-6: uploaded images deleted within twenty-four hours
nodes.norm_label: nfr-6: uploaded images deleted within twenty-four hours

nodes.label: NFR-8: per-run observability (step count, token spend, outcome, failure reason)
nodes.norm_label: nfr-8: per-run observability (step count, token spend, outcome, failure reason)

nodes.label: Bring-your-own-key
nodes.rationale: The release valve for launch-day traffic: it decouples cost from popularity on the one day popularity spikes.

nodes.label: Quadratic screenshot-history cost
nodes.rationale: Each step resends the history: forty steps at 1,570 tokens per screenshot send about 1.3M input tokens cumulatively, roughly $3.50 per image with caching and $14.50 without.

nodes.label: Risk: cost per run under real traffic
nodes.norm_label: risk: cost per run under real traffic
nodes.rationale: Bounded by the step cap and metering, but the cap has to be set from measured runs.

nodes.label: Ideation unit economics estimate ($3-6 per image)
nodes.norm_label: ideation unit economics estimate ($3-6 per image)
nodes.rationale: Forty screenshot-driven steps resend their history for about 1.3M cumulative input tokens, mostly cached, plus ~30K output; assume the top of the range. The 2x tier past 272K input is charged per request, and a single request tops out near 63K.

nodes.label: Astra agent loop
nodes.rationale: Runs on the Responses API because Chat Completions does not support function calling with Astra; a step cap, a spend cap, model-produced narration and an explicit reasoning effort are not optional.

nodes.label: Limit tests (each limit hit, not reasoned about)
nodes.norm_label: limit tests (each limit hit, not reasoned about)

nodes.label: 272K-token long-request pricing tier
nodes.rationale: Billed per request at 2x input and cache rates and 1.5x output, but forty frames come to about 63K tokens, so the step cap keeps runs far below it; the exposure is cumulative, not per request.

nodes.label: Machine-local cache overflow above 15 requests per minute
nodes.norm_label: machine-local cache overflow above 15 requests per minute
nodes.rationale: Twenty concurrent runs (NFR-4) send more than the threshold in total; whether it counts per cached prefix or across the organisation is unknown, and it decides whether launch-day traffic lands in the caching-working or caching-broken cost row.

nodes.label: Per-run structured log line
nodes.rationale: One table answers every launch-day question; frames are not logged, instructions are truncated, keys never appear.

nodes.label: Four run limits (step cap, spend cap, free runs, daily ceiling)
nodes.norm_label: four run limits (step cap, spend cap, free runs, daily ceiling)
nodes.rationale: The free allowance uses a signed cookie plus address and is defeatable, so the daily ceiling is what protects spend. A user-supplied key bypasses free runs and the ceiling because it is their money, but not the step or spend caps.

nodes.label: Spike A2: step cap and frame window the cost allows
nodes.norm_label: spike a2: step cap and frame window the cost allows

nodes.label: Spike A4: OpenAI tier vs NFR-4
nodes.norm_label: spike a4: openai tier vs nfr-4

nodes.label: Metered credits business model
nodes.rationale: Plan at $6 per image and treat anything above $8 as a bug; hard-cap steps, cache aggressively, and never go unmetered so one launch-day user cannot cost fifty dollars.

nodes.label: Bounded frame window
nodes.rationale: The first screenshot plus the last few, as a backstop if caching underperforms, at some cost to the model's view of what it already did; the window size comes from spike A2.

nodes.label: Daily ceiling sized against concurrency, not one user
nodes.norm_label: daily ceiling sized against concurrency, not one user
nodes.rationale: Twenty concurrent runs spend about $70 in one ten-minute wave, so a ceiling near fifty dollars trips on the first wave; honest visitors are bounded by the allowance (~$10.50), determined ones by the ceiling, set on day 4 from measured cost.

nodes.label: Image resolution vs screenshot viewport
nodes.rationale: The photograph stays at full resolution in Photopea and in the exported PSD, while the screenshot is always the 1440x900 viewport; the no-downscaling rule is about screenshots, not the photograph.

nodes.label: No unit tests of model behaviour
nodes.norm_label: no unit tests of model behaviour
nodes.rationale: The model is not deterministic, and pretending otherwise wastes days the project does not have.

nodes.label: OpenAI tier rate limit as the concurrency ceiling
nodes.norm_label: openai tier rate limit as the concurrency ceiling
nodes.rationale: Tier 1 allows 500,000 tokens per minute and image tokens count, so twenty runs exhaust it before the server notices; raising the tier has a lead time the team does not control.

nodes.label: Prompt caching strategy
nodes.rationale: Cached reads at $1/M bring ~$13 of input down to ~$2; this needs a byte-stable tool array, the 1,024-token minimum prefix, the 30-minute TTL and an append-only loop.

nodes.label: Explicit reasoning.effort via configuration_update
nodes.rationale: Astra's default is undocumented and none returns HTTP 400; the loop runs at low and raises to high for planning without disturbing the cached prefix.

nodes.label: Screenshot policy: 1440x900, detail original, no downscaling
nodes.norm_label: screenshot policy: 1440x900, detail original, no downscaling
nodes.rationale: The integration guide warns against high and low detail and names 1440x900 as a well-performing resolution; downscaling would force coordinate remapping, a bug generator. A frame costs about 1,570 tokens.

nodes.label: FR-10: live view of the editor (at least one frame per 2 s, at most 3 s behind)
nodes.norm_label: fr-10: live view of the editor (at least one frame per 2 s, at most 3 s behind)

nodes.label: FR-11: progress as step count against the cap with plain-words current action
nodes.norm_label: fr-11: progress as step count against the cap with plain-words current action

nodes.label: FR-13: cancel at any point and keep the partial result
nodes.norm_label: fr-13: cancel at any point and keep the partial result

nodes.label: FR-14: survive a page reload by resuming the live view
nodes.norm_label: fr-14: survive a page reload by resuming the live view

nodes.label: FR-15: show the running session cost in credits
nodes.norm_label: fr-15: show the running session cost in credits

nodes.label: FR-20: apply a typed mid-run correction without discarding completed work
nodes.norm_label: fr-20: apply a typed mid-run correction without discarding completed work

nodes.label: FR-21: acknowledge a correction visibly within three seconds
nodes.norm_label: fr-21: acknowledge a correction visibly within three seconds

nodes.label: FR-22: show accepted corrections in a visible list
nodes.norm_label: fr-22: show accepted corrections in a visible list

nodes.label: FR-23: correction that undoes work already done (P2)
nodes.norm_label: fr-23: correction that undoes work already done (p2)

nodes.label: FR-29: list the layers on the page after the run
nodes.norm_label: fr-29: list the layers on the page after the run

nodes.label: FR-3: reject invalid input with a specific reason
nodes.norm_label: fr-3: reject invalid input with a specific reason

nodes.label: Code-execution tool over a persistent Playwright session
nodes.norm_label: code-execution tool over a persistent playwright session
nodes.rationale: The planned mechanism because OpenAI recommends it for Astra and it is likely more reliable; the editor still has no usable API, so the competence exercised is still a forty-step GUI task.

nodes.label: computer tool (GA)
nodes.rationale: Kept as the fallback; its GA definition carries no display size or environment fields, and every computer-tool example in the guide is pinned to the previous-generation model.

nodes.label: Contract tests
nodes.rationale: Run against both the fake and the real implementation of each contract so the fakes cannot drift.

nodes.label: Live frame pump
nodes.rationale: Periodic PNGs over the event stream cost nothing to build and degrade gracefully where a stalled video does not; kept separate from model frames so demo smoothness is not coupled to the token bill.

nodes.label: HTTP API surface (Contract 3)
nodes.rationale: Server-sent events rather than WebSockets for the browser leg: the stream is one-directional, corrections go over a normal POST, and SSE reconnects by itself.

nodes.label: Orchestrator
nodes.rationale: The only component that talks to the model, so a model change does not leak past it.

nodes.label: Native steering via response.steer
nodes.rationale: Astra-only, so it is genuine model leverage and the beat the demo is built around; steers do not undo actions, are connection-local, and the connection lives at most sixty minutes.

nodes.label: Single-page web application
nodes.rationale: Rendered from the API process for one deployment and one origin; run state lives server-side keyed by runId, and the correction box is always visible because it is the most important control.

nodes.label: Spike A0: code execution or the computer tool
nodes.norm_label: spike a0: code execution or the computer tool
nodes.rationale: Day 0 despite being short because, with A4, it can still change the plan; both mechanisms run against the same three-edit sequence.

nodes.label: Spike A3: does native mid-turn steering work
nodes.norm_label: spike a3: does native mid-turn steering work

nodes.label: Stub HTTP server serving Contract 3 from fakeRun
nodes.norm_label: stub http server serving contract 3 from fakerun

nodes.label: Fakes-first development
nodes.rationale: Each stream first ships a fake of its own contract so the whole system runs end to end on day 0 and a real implementation lands as a one-line swap; the single decision that makes three-way parallelism possible.

nodes.label: Single-container continuous deployment
nodes.rationale: Deployed continuously from main from day 0 with no staging, because the first deployment is the one most likely to eat an afternoon and finding that out on day 5 misses launches.

nodes.label: Single long-lived server process (not serverless)
nodes.rationale: A run is a stateful conversation lasting minutes that holds a browser session and streams frames; it cannot be resumed from nothing on a cold invocation.

nodes.label: Steering fallback: inject the correction at the next step boundary
nodes.norm_label: steering fallback: inject the correction at the next step boundary
nodes.rationale: Written first on day 1 so steering is never on the critical path; completed work survives because the editor holds the state. It is not Astra-specific, so if only it ships steering is described as a loop feature.

nodes.label: Upload validation before session creation
nodes.rationale: Format by magic bytes, size by actual body length, dimensions from the header; a browser session opened for an upload that was always going to be rejected is a bill paid for nothing.

nodes.label: FR-16: per-user history of past runs (P2, deferred by the non-goals)
nodes.norm_label: fr-16: per-user history of past runs (p2, deferred by the non-goals)
nodes.rationale: The product brief's non-goals rule out both history and accounts, so it waits until those are revisited after launch.

nodes.label: FR-2: free-text instruction of up to 500 characters
nodes.norm_label: fr-2: free-text instruction of up to 500 characters

nodes.label: FR-28: flattened PNG preview alongside the PSD
nodes.norm_label: fr-28: flattened png preview alongside the psd

nodes.label: FR-4: three worked example instructions that fill the box on click
nodes.norm_label: fr-4: three worked example instructions that fill the box on click

nodes.label: NFR-3: a run starts within five seconds of the button
nodes.norm_label: nfr-3: a run starts within five seconds of the button

nodes.label: NFR-7: page works at 1280 px and above; mobile out of scope
nodes.norm_label: nfr-7: page works at 1280 px and above; mobile out of scope

nodes.label: Photopea licence question (answered: automated and commercial use permitted)
nodes.norm_label: photopea licence question (answered: automated and commercial use permitted)
nodes.rationale: Photopea's terms let anyone use it for any purpose for free and say nothing about bots or automation; what remains is commercial, since removing ads needs a Distributor account from EUR 60 a month.

nodes.label: Risk: the scripting escape hatch
nodes.rationale: Scripting the retouching decisions through Photopea's Photoshop-compatible interface would let any model do the job and void the premise; holding the line is a discipline problem, not a technical one.

nodes.label: ag-psd fallback
nodes.rationale: MIT library that writes layered PSDs from Node with no browser; the floor, not a plan: nothing to watch or steer, no model leverage, and the launch copy stops claiming computer use.

nodes.label: Browser provider shortlist (Browserbase, Anchor, Hyperbrowser, Steel)
nodes.norm_label: browser provider shortlist (browserbase, anchor, hyperbrowser, steel)
nodes.rationale: All four expose a live-view iframe and CDP from one session-create call; Steel's Launch tier is disqualified because its fifteen-minute session cap equals the run ceiling, and Anchor's human handoff is for a later version.

nodes.label: Browserbase
nodes.rationale: Default choice: the cheapest entry tier ($20/mo) that covers twenty concurrent runs, with a six-hour session length nowhere near binding.

nodes.label: ComputerAction type
nodes.rationale: Mirrors the computer tool's action schema exactly so a computer_call passes through without translation and the fallback stays a swap.

nodes.label: Editor adapter
nodes.rationale: The only component that knows which editor is driven; everything else sees Contract 1.

nodes.label: Embedded Photopea driven by the user (fallback product)
nodes.norm_label: embedded photopea driven by the user (fallback product)
nodes.rationale: Saves the hosted browser, but the agent writes scripts rather than looking; a different, weaker product that the editor fallback turns into.

nodes.label: Hosted Chrome session over CDP
nodes.rationale: A cross-origin iframe gives the parent page no pixels and the agent's entire input is pixels, so the editor must run in a browser the server controls; sessions need at least twenty minutes, concurrency and ideally a live view.

nodes.label: Photopea
nodes.rationale: Chosen because PSD is its native in-memory model rather than an export target, so it emits real layered files where Figma, Canva and Polotno cannot; it needs no account, key or contract and can be framed from any origin.

nodes.label: Photopea Action Manager stub (stringIDToTypeID lookup table)
nodes.norm_label: photopea action manager stub (stringidtotypeid lookup table)
nodes.rationale: Closes the usual Photoshop escape hatch of dropping to action descriptors, and several selection and colour calls silently do nothing from script, so the judgement work is not scriptable even if wanted.

nodes.label: Photopea Distributor account
nodes.rationale: Free embedding shows ads that would appear in the product and the demo recording; from EUR 60 for 30 days at 1,000 frame-loads, bought on day 0 because it has a signup lead time.

nodes.label: Photopea postMessage protocol
nodes.rationale: A String runs as a script and an ArrayBuffer opens as a file, sidestepping the CORS requirement of loading by URL; exports come back as bytes with no filename, MIME type or correlation id, identified by the 8BPS magic.

nodes.label: Photopea known traps
nodes.rationale: Trap 1 ("done" is not a reliable terminator) was confirmed from Photopea's shipped bundle; traps 2-6 (ES3 dialect, poisoned interpreter, silent no-ops, font delay, boot latency) are unreproduced third-party recon and remain warnings until spike B1.

nodes.label: Spike B0: buy the Distributor account and re-read the terms
nodes.norm_label: spike b0: buy the distributor account and re-read the terms
nodes.rationale: No longer gates anything now the licence question is answered; what is left is a purchase with a signup lead time.

nodes.label: Spike B1: verify the image-in, PSD-out round trip
nodes.norm_label: spike b1: verify the image-in, psd-out round trip

nodes.label: Spike B2: Browserbase signup and cold-start measurement
nodes.norm_label: spike b2: browserbase signup and cold-start measurement
nodes.rationale: No longer a comparison: create one real session, confirm the live view and CDP, and measure cold start, which nobody publishes.

nodes.label: Requirement-level exclusions (no accounts, no in-app editing, no undo, PSD-only output, no internationalisation)
nodes.norm_label: requirement-level exclusions (no accounts, no in-app editing, no undo, psd-only output, no internationalisation)
nodes.rationale: The product brief's non-goals are binding on the PRD; the free allowance is enforced without identity, and the app shows the run and hands back a file rather than offering editing.

nodes.label: Product non-goals (no image generation, no batch/API/integrations, no accounts beyond metering, no mobile, no own editor, no presets)
nodes.norm_label: product non-goals (no image generation, no batch/api/integrations, no accounts beyond metering, no mobile, no own editor, no presets)
nodes.rationale: Stated so nobody builds them in the six build days available; a per-client house style is the obvious second product, not the first.

nodes.label: Unique app.echoToOE sentinel per scripted call
nodes.norm_label: unique app.echotooe sentinel per scripted call
nodes.rationale: Some operations emit their own "done" mid-script, so waiting for it desynchronises; a sentinel timeout means reload the frame, not retry, because a crashed script poisons the interpreter while echoToOE still answers.

nodes.label: Export-then-destroy session disposal
nodes.rationale: The session holds the only copy of the work, so FR-12 and FR-13 are unsatisfiable if teardown wins the race; on the error path export is best-effort and must not block the teardown, because a leaked session is a leaked bill.

nodes.label: Fifteen-minute run ceiling
nodes.rationale: The single ceiling everywhere: the sixty-minute WebSocket lifetime is an outer bound and the twenty-minute provider session is margin; sizing the step cap against sixty would make it four times too large.

nodes.label: Scripted vs GUI-driven split (the line that protects the premise)
nodes.norm_label: scripted vs gui-driven split (the line that protects the premise)
nodes.rationale: Loading, layer naming, export and viewport resets are scripted; selecting, masking, choosing adjustments and judging the edit are driven through the GUI, because scripted retouching decisions could be written by any model.

nodes.label: Self-hosted Playwright remote Chrome (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Not a fallback that always works: a watchable, interruptible remote Chrome is weeks of work arbitrating human takeover and keeping raw CDP (Runtime.evaluate, cookies) away from the user's browser; if no provider works, the product changes.

nodes.label: Pre-warmed editor sessions
nodes.rationale: Reported boot (~2 s) plus first round trip (~5 s) overruns NFR-3's five-second budget, so warming the session before the button is load-bearing and the first thing to measure.

nodes.label: Structural agent security controls
nodes.rationale: Make the bad action impossible: a network allow-list to the editor origin, no credentials in the session, the instruction and image treated as untrusted input, and sessions destroyed after every run.

nodes.label: Contest outcome against the four inferred criteria
nodes.norm_label: contest outcome against the four inferred criteria
nodes.rationale: Model leverage is the reason to build this and creativity follows from the inversion; execution is the weak score and the one thing six days of work can move.

nodes.label: GPT-6 Astra
nodes.rationale: 72.6% vs 65.7% on OSWorld V2-Offline separates an agent that can hold a forty-step GUI task together from one that cannot; swapping it out removes the product. It is text-output only and cannot generate images.

nodes.label: Layerhand
nodes.rationale: Three properties in order of importance: the output is editable (the product), the work is visible (trust mechanism and demo), the work is steerable (corrected mid-run like a junior retoucher).

nodes.label: Async tool calling (primitive)
nodes.rationale: Dead: an orchestration ergonomics win that a job queue replicates and the user cannot feel.

nodes.label: Computer use (primitive)
nodes.rationale: The highest-leverage primitive and the best silent GIF; desktop hosting, not computer use, made Round 1 unshippable.

nodes.label: Computer use x mid-turn steering (Round 9)
nodes.rationale: Crossing the two surviving primitives passes the Swap Test on both axes at once; the desktop scope gate falls away once the target is web-based professional software.

nodes.label: Hosted-browser computer use (Round 2)
nodes.rationale: Removes the desktop VM fleet, but pointed at services it lands in crowded startup categories; the lesson is to point it at software instead.

nodes.label: Mid-turn steering (primitive)
nodes.rationale: Passes visibly because elsewhere changing your mind means cancel and re-prompt; it needs a generation long enough to interrupt and an artifact visible enough to see it going wrong.

nodes.label: Million-token single-pass context (primitive)
nodes.rationale: Clears the Swap Test only for inconsistency tasks: retrieval needs a query, and a contradiction has none.

nodes.label: Persisted reasoning and notes (primitive)
nodes.rationale: Dead: Astra has no cross-conversation memory, so persistence built on top of it works on any model.

nodes.label: Programmatic tool calling and orchestration (primitive)
nodes.rationale: Dead: a cost and latency optimisation; batch work that does pass does so for whole-corpus reasoning, not loop-writing.

nodes.label: Steerable financial model built in Sheets
nodes.norm_label: steerable financial model built in sheets

nodes.label: Idea shortlist scoring
nodes.rationale: Layerhand scores 27 with the highest ceiling and the shakiest floor (execution 3); a zero on leverage or execution would disqualify.

nodes.label: WebMCP
nodes.rationale: Dead by design: an open standard that decouples the page from the model scores zero on model leverage; worth it only as a surface attached to an Astra-only capability.

nodes.label: Indirect prompt injection risk
nodes.rationale: Astra's system card estimates an 8.5% attack success rate, and a confirmation policy barely moved unauthorised transactions (6.8%) or data exfiltration (4.3%), so asking the agent to confirm is not a control.

nodes.label: PRD: Layerhand
nodes.rationale: Requirements are numbered FR/NFR so issues, commits and tests can cite them; P0 blocks the launch, P1 makes it poor, P2 comes after the launch if at all.

nodes.label: Product: Layerhand
nodes.rationale: The strategy document: problem, wedge, business model, and the conditions under which the project stops.

nodes.label: Product Hunt ideas: GPT-6 Astra Challenge
nodes.norm_label: product hunt ideas: gpt-6 astra challenge
nodes.rationale: Ten progressive rounds, each picking capability primitives, generating unfiltered, then applying the Swap Test and kill gates; scope killed more ideas than any other gate. It counts five working days but defers to the PRD schedule's six build days.

nodes.label: TRD: Layerhand
nodes.rationale: Describes how Layerhand is built and how it is cut into pieces three people can build at the same time over six days.

nodes.label: Inferred judging rubric (WebMCP Challenge criteria)
nodes.rationale: OpenAI published no judging criteria, so ideas are scored on the four equally weighted WebMCP Challenge criteria plus launch legibility and showcase-ability, an inference from the nearest comparable contest.

nodes.label: Ideation kill gates (scope, crowding)
nodes.rationale: Scope (five build days, no hosted desktop VM fleet) and crowding (existing startup categories, prior hackathon winners) removed ideas that passed the Swap Test.

nodes.label: Swap Test
nodes.rationale: Swap Astra for another model and ask whether the product gets slightly worse or stops existing; applied to user-visible behaviour, never to the implementation, because judges score the product.

nodes.label: Text-only inversion
nodes.rationale: Astra cannot generate an image but can make one by operating an image editor, and what comes back is a layered file, an edit history no diffusion model can produce.

nodes.label: Web-based professional software unlock
nodes.rationale: Round 1's fatal gate was "desktop", not computer use; GUI-locked, API-poor web apps such as Figma, Google Sheets and Photopea run in a hosted browser with no VM fleet or licence server.

nodes.label: Unattended-run system prompt
nodes.rationale: Astra tends to stop early and ask, and over-obeys instruction files, so the prompt says the run is unattended, tells it to carry the task to completion, and carries no decorative prohibitions.

nodes.label: FR-25: PSD opens without error in Photoshop, Affinity Photo and GIMP
nodes.norm_label: fr-25: psd opens without error in photoshop, affinity photo and gimp

nodes.label: FR-26: every layer named in human words
nodes.norm_label: fr-26: every layer named in human words

nodes.norm_label: fr-30: public landing page with the differentiator and a silent demo loop

nodes.norm_label: fr-31: email capture live and collecting before launch day

nodes.norm_label: fr-32: thirty-second silent demo recording usable on product hunt

nodes.norm_label: fr-33: product hunt assets (tagline, description, gallery images, first maker comment)

nodes.label: Launch acceptance checklist (evening of September 17)
nodes.rationale: Every line is checked by someone who did not build it; the unread contest rules gate the launch rather than following it.

nodes.label: Launch schedule (September 12-18, launch Friday 12:01am PT)
nodes.rationale: Friday is outside the Tuesday/Wednesday launch slot, but Wednesday would cost two of six build days and Tuesday three, freezing on the evening of the day-2 go/no-go itself, so the build days win. The ideation doc defers to this six-day count.

nodes.label: NFR-1: reliability, eight of ten test runs complete unattended with a valid layered file
nodes.norm_label: nfr-1: reliability, eight of ten test runs complete unattended with a valid layered file
nodes.rationale: Measured, not estimated, and re-measured the evening of day 5; the number the launch decision turns on.

nodes.label: Single-screen core flow
nodes.rationale: Step 5, typing a correction mid-run and seeing the next actions bend rather than restart, is the product; if it is buried the demo has no centre and the launch has no hook.

nodes.label: Risk: reliability of long GUI control
nodes.norm_label: risk: reliability of long gui control
nodes.rationale: Forty-plus unattended steps in a dense professional interface on an unseen image is the whole technical bet.

nodes.label: Judged-well criteria (differentiator stated after a silent viewing; layer stack survives a retoucher's inspection)
nodes.norm_label: judged-well criteria (differentiator stated after a silent viewing; layer stack survives a retoucher's inspection)

nodes.label: Launch audience risk (no waitlist)
nodes.rationale: Launch mechanics are unforgiving and there is no waitlist, so the audience is a build task with an owner; where it comes from is still an open question.

nodes.label: Must-be-true launch criteria (product brief)
nodes.rationale: Eight of ten unattended runs (NFR-1) is the number the launch decision turns on; the day-2 go/no-go asks less, one scripted three-edit sequence.

nodes.label: Open question: official contest rules
nodes.rationale: The rules sit behind a login wall and are unread: whether a public repository, an open-source licence or a demo video is required is unknown, and it gates the launch.

nodes.label: Before-committing checks (deadline and prize terms, Photopea terms and trademark, waitlist)
nodes.norm_label: before-committing checks (deadline and prize terms, photopea terms and trademark, waitlist)
nodes.rationale: Winning launches draw 60%+ of launch-day traffic from a waitlist and the first six hours decide ranking, so the audience is a build task, not an afterthought.

nodes.label: Thirty-second silent demo storyboard
nodes.rationale: The mid-run correction in beat 3 and the hand-dragged mask slider in beat 5 carry the entire pitch; if either cannot be filmed, the product is not ready to launch.

nodes.norm_label: gpt-6 astra challenge (openai x product hunt)

nodes.norm_label: launch tagline: ai retouching that returns a layered psd, not a flat jpeg

nodes.norm_label: spike a1: can the agent complete one edit unattended

nodes.label: Ten-image test set
nodes.rationale: Ten real photographs, each with a written instruction and expectation, run nightly from day 2; the number the launch decision is made on and the only test that can stop the launch, separate from the lower day-2 go/no-go bar.

nodes.label: Day-2 technical go/no-go (kill switch)
nodes.rationale: By end of Monday, September 14 the agent must complete a scripted three-edit sequence unattended and produce a layered file, or the team ships the contradiction finder, which needs no browser infrastructure; decided once, on evidence, and a lower bar than NFR-1.

nodes.label: Layered PSD output (the wedge)
nodes.rationale: Nearly every competing product emits pixels, and a diffusion model cannot emit a layer stack because a layer stack is an edit history, not an image; a difference in kind, so the pitch is the artifact, not better retouching.

nodes.label: Launch artifact (tagline, first comment, demo storyboard)
nodes.norm_label: launch artifact (tagline, first comment, demo storyboard)
nodes.rationale: Written before any code, because the contest judges a launch.

nodes.label: Markdown style guide
nodes.rationale: Balances three goals: source text that is readable and portable, a corpus maintainable over time and across teams, and syntax that is simple and easy to remember.

nodes.label: ATX-style headings
nodes.rationale: Underlined = or - headings are annoying to maintain and leave the level ambiguous. Put a space after the # and a blank line before and after each heading.

nodes.label: Better/Best Rule
nodes.rationale: Documentation review sets a lower bar per change so that more changes happen: reviewers approve quickly, suggest alternatives and start their own follow-ups for substantial changes, and authors capitulate early instead of arguing.

nodes.label: 80-character line limit
nodes.rationale: Follows the convention for code so code-oriented tooling keeps working (Code Search does not soft wrap) and coding and review habits carry over to docs. Links, tables, headings and code blocks are exempt.

nodes.label: Code spans for inline code and escaping
nodes.norm_label: code spans for inline code and escaping
nodes.rationale: Backticks render short code, field names and generic file names literally, and stop fake paths or example URLs from turning into bad autolinks.

nodes.label: Document layout (H1 title, short introduction, [TOC], topics, See also)
nodes.norm_label: document layout (h1 title, short introduction, [toc], topics, see also)
nodes.rationale: The first H1 should match the filename and becomes the page title; a 1-3 sentence introduction orients a newcomer; topics start at H2; miscellaneous links go in a closing See also section.

nodes.label: Explicit link paths (relative only within the same directory)
nodes.norm_label: explicit link paths (relative only within the same directory)
nodes.rationale: Link other Markdown pages by explicit path rather than a fully qualified URL; relative paths are safe within the same directory, but ../ paths into other directories should be avoided.

nodes.label: Fenced code blocks with a declared language
nodes.norm_label: fenced code blocks with a declared language
nodes.rationale: Indented blocks cannot name a language, have ambiguous boundaries and are harder to find in Code Search. Declare the language so neither the highlighter nor the next editor must guess, escape newlines in copyable shell snippets, and indent blocks nested in lists.

nodes.label: Capitalization of titles and headings
nodes.rationale: Defers to the capitalization guidance of the Google Developer Documentation Style Guide.

nodes.label: Use images sparingly, with alt text
nodes.norm_label: use images sparingly, with alt text
nodes.rationale: Plain text gets readers to the point with less distraction; use an image when showing is easier than describing, and describe it for readers who cannot see it.

nodes.label: Informative link titles
nodes.rationale: Readers scan rather than read, and link text such as 'here', 'link' or a bare URL tells them nothing; write the sentence naturally, then wrap its most descriptive phrase.

nodes.label: Lazy list numbering and 4-space nested indent
nodes.norm_label: lazy list numbering and 4-space nested indent
nodes.rationale: Lazy 1. numbering suits long lists that may change, while short stable lists read better fully numbered in source; a 4-space indent keeps wrapped and nested text aligned.

nodes.label: Strongly prefer Markdown to HTML
nodes.rationale: Every HTML hack reduces the readability and portability of the corpus and its usefulness to tools that show the source as plain text or render it; Gitiles does not render HTML.

nodes.label: Preserve original product name capitalization
nodes.rationale: Names of products, tools and binaries keep their original capitalization.

nodes.label: Reference links
nodes.rationale: Split a long link from its use when inlining it would hurt readability, especially in tables, or to reduce duplication; avoid them for short links because they hide the destination. Define them just before the next heading after first use, or at the end of the document when several sections share them, to avoid dangling links.

nodes.label: Single H1 heading
nodes.rationale: One H1 serves as the document title; every later heading is H2 or deeper.

nodes.label: Tables only for two-dimensional data
nodes.rationale: Use a table for uniform data across two dimensions or many parallel items with distinct attributes; poor distribution, unbalanced dimensions or rambling prose in cells signal that a list would serve better.

nodes.label: [TOC] directive after the introduction
nodes.rationale: Use it unless all content is above the fold. Placement matters for screen readers and keyboard users, because [TOC] inserts the table of contents into the DOM wherever the directive appears.

nodes.label: No trailing whitespace (trailing backslash for line breaks)
nodes.norm_label: no trailing whitespace (trailing backslash for line breaks)
nodes.rationale:
CommonMark turns two trailing spaces into a
, but presubmit checks and IDEs strip trailing whitespace; a trailing backslash is explicit, and a blank line between paragraphs usually removes the need.

nodes.label: Unique, complete heading names
nodes.rationale: Link anchors are generated from headings, so unique, fully descriptive names keep those anchors intuitive and clear.

nodes.label: RTK condensed command output
nodes.rationale: Output is condensed to save tokens while keeping every signal, so treat it as the complete result, run commands normally and batch related commands to avoid extra turns.

nodes.label: .agents/skills/ skills directory
nodes.rationale: Holds installed and local skills in one place; .claude/skills/ symlinks to it instead of keeping a copy.

nodes.label: AGENTS.md (agent instruction entry point)
nodes.rationale: Pure @-import manifest with no inline prose: it pulls in four docs/agents pages (Andrej Karpathy skills, graphify, RTK, skills) and the Markdown style guide, keeping each concern in its own file. docs/agents/rules.md is not among the imports, although that page names AGENTS.md as the entry point. CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md are symlinks to it, so edits go to AGENTS.md only.

nodes.label: Andrej Karpathy Skills (behavioral guidelines)
nodes.rationale: Guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes; they bias toward caution over speed, with judgment allowed for trivial tasks.

nodes.label: Goal-Driven Execution
nodes.rationale: Turn tasks into verifiable goals and loop until verified; strong success criteria allow independent looping while weak ones need constant clarification.

nodes.label: Simplicity First
nodes.rationale: Minimum code that solves the problem and nothing speculative: no unrequested features, single-use abstractions, unrequested configurability or error handling for impossible scenarios.

nodes.label: Surgical Changes
nodes.rationale: Touch only what you must and clean up only your own mess; every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

nodes.label: Think Before Coding
nodes.rationale: Don't assume, don't hide confusion, surface tradeoffs: state assumptions, present competing interpretations, push back when a simpler approach exists, and stop to ask when something is unclear.

nodes.label: Query the graph before reading source
nodes.norm_label: query the graph before reading source
nodes.rationale: graphify query, path and explain return a scoped subgraph, usually much smaller than GRAPH_REPORT.md or raw grep output; the wiki index serves broad navigation and GRAPH_REPORT.md only broad architecture review.

nodes.label: Run graphify update after modifying code
nodes.norm_label: run graphify update after modifying code
nodes.rationale: Keeps the graph current; the update is AST-only, so it has no API cost.

nodes.label: rtk proxy fallback
nodes.rationale: Re-run a command through rtk proxy only when its result is unusable: empty when output was expected, contradicting its exit code, or garbled.

nodes.label: AGENTS.md as the single agent entry point
nodes.norm_label: agents.md as the single agent entry point
nodes.rationale: AGENTS.md is symlinked as CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md, so every agent reads the same instructions. Edit AGENTS.md itself, never either symlink.

nodes.label: Minimum viable documentation
nodes.rationale: A small set of fresh, accurate docs beats a sprawling assembly in disrepair; authors own their docs as they own tests and delete cruft often, in small batches.

nodes.label: How it was verified (pull request template section)
nodes.norm_label: how it was verified (pull request template section)
nodes.rationale: Asks for the commands that were run and what they printed, not a claim that it should work.

nodes.label: Prettier owns syntax, not prose
nodes.rationale: bun run lint checks the whole tree and lint-staged fixes staged files on commit, so do not hand-format around it. printWidth applies to code and proseWrap is left at preserve, so Prettier never rewraps a Markdown paragraph: the 80-character limit is the author's to keep and nothing checks it.

nodes.label: Adobe Photoshop API v2
nodes.rationale: /v2/execute-actions runs Photoshop Actions server-side and /v2/create-composite returns a layered PSD with no browser or GUI; only an enterprise contract stands in the way, a commercial moat Adobe can remove at will.

nodes.label: BRIA AI
nodes.rationale: Self-serve image_to_psd endpoint from $0.018; which layers it emits is unverified, and if it carries named, masked and adjustment layers the remaining gap is closed.

nodes.label: Flat-output competitors (Photoroom, Clipdrop, Pixelcut, Claid, Pixelbin, remove.bg, Evoto, Imagen AI, Aftershoot, BoxBrownie)
nodes.norm_label: flat-output competitors (photoroom, clipdrop, pixelcut, claid, pixelbin, remove.bg, evoto, imagen ai, aftershoot, boxbrownie)

nodes.label: Flat-output problem in AI retouching
nodes.rationale: Almost every AI retouching tool returns a flattened image that cannot absorb the client's next change, so the retoucher redoes the work and the AI saved nothing; the gap is the format of the output, not quality.

nodes.label: Human retouching price ceiling ($0.39-$2.00 per image)
nodes.norm_label: human retouching price ceiling ($0.39-$2.00 per image)
nodes.rationale: At $3.50 of model spend per image Layerhand costs five to nine times a human and about two hundred times BRIA; the retouching line item is already small.

nodes.label: Missing demand signal for layered-PSD delivery
nodes.norm_label: missing demand signal for layered-psd delivery
nodes.rationale: None of thirteen priced outsourcers markets layered delivery; photographers complain about consistency and rework, which argues for a deterministic QC pipeline rather than an agent working by eye.

nodes.label: Retouch4me
nodes.rationale: Partly layered: real Photoshop layers and masks, separate or merged at the user's choice, but no adjustment layers.

nodes.label: Target users: e-commerce photo teams, real-estate photographers, freelance retouchers
nodes.norm_label: target users: e-commerce photo teams, real-estate photographers, freelance retouchers
nodes.rationale: Aimed at people who already pay for retouching and already work in layers; consumers do not want a PSD and a free consumer tier breaks the unit economics.

nodes.label: Commercial gate (risk 1: the commercial case vs the survey)
nodes.norm_label: commercial gate (risk 1: the commercial case vs the survey)
nodes.rationale: A decision rather than a monitored risk, answered before any code because it decides which product the code is for; the readings are a contest entry, a brief repointed at the self-serve gap once BRIA's output is checked, or the runner-up.

nodes.label: Competition survey (twenty-six products)
nodes.rationale: Checked against the products' own format enums and documentation rather than comparison articles; it retracts the earlier claim that every AI photo tool hands you pixels.

nodes.label: Remaining gap: no self-serve single-pass PSD known to be named, masked and adjustment-layered
nodes.norm_label: remaining gap: no self-serve single-pass psd known to be named, masked and adjustment-layered
nodes.rationale: Narrower than the pitch: Adobe's API delivers it only under an enterprise contract, and BRIA is self-serve but its PSD layers are unverified; if BRIA carries all three, the gap is closed.
